paras: The threatened lynching of Charles S. Burns took place on Fore street in Portland, Maine, on the afternoon of January 15, 1903, when a street crowd pursued Burns, a Black man, shouting "Lynch him" and "Kill him." Burns, who had been accused of chasing a restaurant keeper's wife with knives, took refuge in a drug store and was arrested. He was not harmed, and the next day he pleaded guilty to intoxication and was sentenced to thirty days in jail.

According to the Portland Daily Press, Burns was intoxicated when he went into Thomas Jones's restaurant at 221 Fore street to get something to eat. The paper reported that after a while he said he wanted to "carve some one" and produced a knife.

In the Press's account, Burns chased Mrs. Martha Jones, the proprietor's wife, out of the restaurant with a butcher knife in each hand after smashing things inside. A Portland dispatch printed in the Daily Kennebec Journal said instead that he carried two knives and a revolver, threatened to "kill somebody," and that Mrs. Jones took refuge in a nearby grocery.

When Burns ran into the street, a crowd followed him; the Press said it shouted "Lynch him" and "Kill him," while the Kennebec Journal called it only "a threatening crowd." Burns took refuge in Stone's drug store, where he was arrested.
On January 16 Burns pleaded guilty in court to a charge of intoxication and received thirty days in jail. No report of any arrest or inquiry concerning the crowd appears in the coverage.

Coverage came only from white Maine papers, and no report was found in the Black press. The Portland Daily Press ran the story under the headline "NEGRO WITH KNIVES. Almost Precipitated a Riot on Fore Street," opening with the statement that "a negro ran amuck" and treating the crowd's lynch cries as a near riot provoked by Burns. The Augusta-based Kennebec Journal printed the dispatch on its front page as "REVOLVER AND TWO KNIVES. Bad Negro Heavily Armed Under Arrest in Portland," giving his name as "Charles B. Burns of Boston."
Neither paper questioned the crowd's conduct, and the Press's court column the next day described Burns only as "the negro who, on Thursday, chased a woman on Fore street."

The two reports differ on Burns's middle initial and home, on whether he also carried a revolver, and on whether Mrs. Jones was chased into the street or sheltered in a grocery. The Press, a local paper that followed the case into court, mentioned only knives in both of its reports.

bases: A street crowd pursued Burns shouting "Lynch him" and "Kill him" until he took refuge in a drug store and was arrested [A1], with a 'threatening crowd' also reported by a second paper [A2]; no one was attacked, so this is a threatened lynching only.

No one was killed: the crowd pursued and threatened Burns but he reached a drug store and was arrested, then jailed for intoxication [A1][A2][A3]. The crowd's cries of 'Lynch him' are reported by one paper only [A1].

Two papers with differing details (Portland Daily Press and a Portland dispatch in the Kennebec Journal) agree that Burns brandished knives in a Fore street restaurant, a threatening crowd followed him, and he was arrested in a drug store [A1][A2]; the lynch cries rest on [A1] alone.

accounts.gist: Burns, 'of Boston,' armed with two knives and a revolver, threatened to 'kill somebody'; Mrs. Jones took refuge in a grocery; a 'threatening crowd' followed him to a drug store, where he was arrested.

framing.detail: The Portland Daily Press headlined 'NEGRO WITH KNIVES' and said he 'ran amuck,' presenting the crowd's lynch cries as a near-'riot' caused by Burns without comment on the crowd.
The Kennebec Journal headlined 'Bad Negro Heavily Armed Under Arrest in Portland' and mentioned the crowd only as 'threatening.'
